title: I Built a Product for 10,000 Users. Here’s Why 90% of Them Left.

Product Management User Experience User Retention Onboarding Activation Rate I Built a Product for 10,000 Users. Here’s Why 90% of Them Left. Tohbie Adelaja 5 min read · Oct 27, 2026 -- 3 Listen Share That’s me, Tohbie Let me tell you about the most humbling moment of my career. I spent four months building a product that was technically functional, operationally sound, and strategically aligned with every OKR we had set. And it was failing the exact people it was designed to serve. Here’s what nobody tells you when you’re learning to build products: the systems we create are never neutral. They carry assumptions, they encode priorities, and when those assumptions are wrong, the people you’re trying to help pay the price. I learned this the hard way. This is what I wish someone had told me earlier. Most of us are not actually building for users. We’re building for the story we want to tell investors, the board, or our LinkedIn followers. The user becomes a data point, a retention curve, a number on a slide. I’ve been guilty of this. I’ve sat in sprint planning meetings where we debated button colors and A/B test results while completely ignoring the fact that our most loyal users were sending us support tickets that read like cries for help. “I don’t understand why this takes so long.” “I’ve tried to do this three times and it keeps resetting.” “Is there a human I can talk to?” We called those “edge cases.” They were not edge cases, they were the product telling us the truth. The uncomfortable reality: When 90% of your users leave, they’re not the problem. Your system is! They just have better things to do than debug your assumptions for you. The Insight: Every Product Has a “Desperation Point” Here’s the non-obvious framing that changed how I see everything. Every product has a moment, usually early in the user journey where the user is essentially asking: “Is this worth my time, or should I go back to how I use to do things before?” I call this the Desperation Point. We built product for users to become desperate, rather than building the system to be deliberate for the user to stay. I’ve seen product being clumsy, manipulative, or simply confusing at exactly the wrong moment. Imagine the onboarding flow that asks for 6 permissions before delivering any value, the pricing page that hides the real cost until the fourth or fifth step or the feature that technically works but makes the user feel stupid. At the Desperation Point, the system reveals what it actually values. And most of the time, it values metrics more than humans . I didn’t understand this until I started talking to the users who left. The ones who just… disappeared. The silent majority. A Useful Framework Then I built a simple framework to catch this before it costs you your users. It’s five questions. I run it on every product I touch now. You should too. The Desperation Audit: Where is the first moment of real value? How many steps does it take for a new user to get something they actually wanted? If it’s more than three, you have a problem. What does the system ask for before it gives? Every permission request, every form field, every “create an account to continue” is a withdrawal from the user’s trust account. Are you making deposits first? What happens when the user fails? Not if. When. Does the system help them recover, or does it punish them for not being perfect? Who is this system assuming exists? What device do they have? What language do they speak? How much time do they have? What privileges does your product assume the user has, and who does that exclude? If you were a user, would you trust this product after 60 seconds? Be honest. Not proud. Honest. When I ran this audit on the product that lost 90% of its users, the answers were brutal. We were asking for too much, too early. We were making value conditional on data collection. We were punishing users for normal behavior. And we were assuming a user had high-speed internet, a modern phone, and infinite patience. That user didn’t exist, at least not in this part of the Milky Way. The Receipts: What Actually Happened When We Fixed It We didn’t rebuild the product, we simply rebuilt the assumptions. We moved the first moment of value from step six to step one. We stopped asking for permissions we didn’t need yet. We added a human-readable error message to every failure state. We tested the product on a 2G connection on a budget Android phone. Within six weeks: Activation rate (users who completed the core action at least once) went from 11% to 43%. Support tickets related to “confusion” dropped by 62%. Voluntary retention at day 30 improved by 3.2x. This product didn’t get “better” in any flashy way. The codebase was still messy. Beautiful face, I mean UI, back end is terrific. But the system stopped asking users to prove themselves before it gave them anything. That’s the difference. That’s the whole game. The Implications: What to Do This Tuesday If you’re building anything, a product, a service, a workflow, a team: here’s what I want you to take away. Stop celebrating your green dashboards. They’re lying to you. A green dashboard just means the people who stayed are willing to tolerate your system. It says nothing about the people who left. Find your Desperation Point.
